To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
citation distributions across scientific fields are very similar and that the differences in citation practices across fields are about 13% in size.

the effect of differences in citation practice represents about 13 % of total citation inequality and that the two-parameter normalization method reduces this inequality to a level very near to the minimum possible given the data.

the IDCP method is an effective way to evaluate the performance of normalization procedures, and that the two-parameter procedure is the best normalization scheme in the sense that it yields the smallest possible effect of differences in citation practice.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of how to compare scientific fields in terms of their citation impact.
a very specific problem of citation analysis, namely the problem of comparing citation counts across scientific fields.

the development of normalization procedures that are able to suppress the effect of citation practices on citation inequality, thus allowing a fair comparison of citation counts across different fields.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the two-parameter normalization procedure is the best one in the long run, but the traditional normalization procedure is a good second best.
, in the absence of better data, the best normalization procedure is the two-parameter scheme, while the mean normalization procedure can be considered as a good alternative.
the two-parameter normalization procedure and the traditional mean-based procedure are the best normalization methods, but they are not very far apart in their performance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, while the effect of differences in citation practice is not negligible, it can be reduced to a very low level by the application of appropriate normalization procedures.

the IDCP method is a powerful tool for the rigorous evaluation of normalization procedures, and that the best normalization procedures perform reasonably well, reducing citation inequality to levels that are very close to the theoretical minimum.

, in the context of our study, the differences in citation practices among scientific domains have only a minor effect on citation inequality, and that this effect can be reduced to a very low level by the application of a simple normalization procedure.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the choice of the normalization procedure has a limited impact on the results, and the most important factor to consider is the quality of the classification system used to define the scientific sub-fields.

, given the current classification system, it is possible to reduce citation inequality to a level that is close to the minimum possible, but that the best performance is achieved by the two-parameter normalization procedure.
, in the absence of a better alternative, normalization procedures based on sub-field mean citations should be preferred over more sophisticated alternatives.
